record.narrative: First iteration prioritizes 12 high-prior, falsifiable comparisons that cover driver mutations, amplifications, synthetic-lethal chromatin-repair relationships, MSI biology, MYC-associated transcription/translation dependency, and one technical library benchmark. Because more negative dependency scores mean stronger dependency, hypotheses expecting stronger dependency are proposed with direction=-1 (raw exposed-minus-comparator negative), while hypotheses expecting weaker dependency are proposed with direction=+1 (raw difference positive). The first six biological probes test direct oncogene dependencies or pathway relationships: KRAS mutation should increase KRAS dependency, and potentially STAT3 dependency through downstream signaling; EGFR amplification and ERBB2 amplification should increase their corresponding dependencies; BRAF V600E, restricted to KRAS wildtype lineages, should increase BRAF dependency; TP53 loss should reduce MDM2 dependency because MDM2 is primarily relevant to p53 regulation. The next four test established or pathway-level synthetic-lethal ideas: SMARCA4 loss should increase SMARCA2 dependency, KEAP1 loss may alter NFE2L2 dependency through NRF2 pathway activation, and MSI-high should increase WRN dependency. MYC amplification probes transcription/replication stress dependencies through DHX9 and RPL11. Finally, an Avana-library contrast for POLR2A serves as a broad technical benchmark for a highly essential gene and helps detect library-specific scaling or confounding before interpreting weaker biological effects. All claims remain unresolved before analysis; effect sizes will be judged against the 10% relative clinical-significance benchmark, uncertainty, and cell counts.

Requesting discovery analysis for all twelve registered hypotheses. This first batch tests direct oncogene dependencies, pathway dependencies, synthetic-lethal relationships, and one technical library benchmark for POLR2A. The signed estimates will be interpreted with direction already incorporated: for dependency scores, a positive signed estimate means the hypothesis direction was supported, while a negative signed estimate means the observed effect is opposite to the proposed hypothesis. I will prioritize effect size relative to the 10% clinical-significance benchmark, 95% interval precision, and comparison-cell sample sizes when these results arrive.

The first discovery batch separates into three very large dependencies, several small/borderline oncogene effects, and several null or opposite small effects. I interpreted all estimates as already signed to the registered direction: for direction=-1 claims, a positive estimate means exposure is associated with a more negative dependency score, i.e., stronger dependency. For direction=+1 claims, a positive estimate means exposure is associated with a less negative score, i.e., weaker dependency. Because a 10% relative effect is clinically meaningful but exact subgroup means are not shown, I used the population outcome means as an approximate scale: most scores around -0.25 correspond to a 10% threshold around 0.025; SMARCA2 around -0.42 gives about 0.042; WRN around -0.30 gives about 0.030; NFE2L2 around -0.09 gives about 0.009.

The clearest accepted findings are H7 and H9. H7 says SMARCA4 loss increases SMARCA2 dependency: the signed estimate is +0.784, with a 95% interval entirely positive and far above the clinical threshold, n=412/1588. This is a very large, robustly signed effect and is biologically coherent as SWI/SNF synthetic lethality. H9 says MSI-high increases WRN dependency: signed +0.790, interval far above threshold, n=130/1870. Although MSI-high has the smaller exposed cell count, the interval is extremely precise relative to the 10% scale and excludes a trivial effect; I accept it as a discovery in this dataset. H8 was hypothesized in the opposite canonical direction: KEAP1 loss increasing NFE2L2 dependency. The signed estimate is -0.796, implying a raw positive contrast, i.e., KEAP1 loss is associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency. The interval is entirely negative, so the registered direction is strongly rejected. However, because this is a huge opposite effect and could reflect biology, coding convention, or a noncanonical data structure, I keep the investigation active and request independent validation for H8 before treating the reversed claim as established.

Most direct driver tests are not yet decisive. H1 KRAS mutation -> KRAS dependency is small but directionally supportive, signed +0.0137, interval [-0.0038,+0.0312]. The upper bound can exceed the approximate 10% threshold, but the point estimate is below it and zero is not excluded, so unresolved active. H3 EGFR amplification -> EGFR dependency is similar: signed +0.0252, interval nearly reaching zero at -0.0003 but extending to +0.0507; it is suggestive but not acceptably precise. H4 ERBB2 amplification is near null with wide uncertainty and could still include a clinically meaningful positive effect, so I defer rather than reject. H5 BRAF V600E in KRAS wildtype gives a signed negative estimate, opposite the expected stronger-dependency direction; importantly, the upper bound is below the approximate positive clinical threshold, so the registered direction is rejected and closed as a main test. H2 STAT3 KRAS effect is small and opposite, and its interval does not support a clinically meaningful positive effect; rejected. H6 TP53 loss -> MDM2 weaker is directionally small positive and imprecise, so unresolved deferred. H10/H11 MYC amplification -> DHX9/RPL11 are small/opposite and their upper bounds are below the approximate positive threshold, so rejected closed. H12 Avana-library benchmark for POLR2A is small and imprecise, so unresolved deferred.

For validation, I choose H8 rather than H7 or H9 because H8 is the surprising large opposite effect. Independent validation will help decide whether to accept a reversed KEAP1-NFE2L2 association or treat it as a sign/coding artifact. I have registered follow-up proposals: ARID1A loss -> SMARCA2 dependency, reversed KEAP1 -> NFE2L2 dependency, SMARCA4 effect within ARID1A co-loss, SMARCA4 effect within the Avana library, BRCA2 loss -> WRN, MSI-high excluding BRCA2 loss, MYC amplification -> TMED10, and TP53 loss -> USP7. These follow-ups refine the accepted synthetic-lethal discoveries, test confounding/library robustness, and explore adjacent pathways. These conclusions are associations within this dataset and not claims of causality or generalizability.

The independent validation resolves the KEAP1/NFE2L2 sign question. The original H8 hypothesis was that KEAP1 loss increases NFE2L2 dependency. Because H8 was registered with direction=-1, a clinically meaningful finding would require a positive signed estimate. The discovery R8 is negative and the validation R13 is also negative with an independent interval entirely below zero: signed estimate -0.8096, interval -0.8392 to -0.7800. In raw terms this means KEAP1-loss cells have higher NFE2L2 dependency scores than KEAP1-intact cells, i.e. weaker NFE2L2 dependency. Since the NFE2L2 population mean magnitude is only about 0.093, this opposite-direction effect is far above the approximate 10% clinical benchmark. I therefore reject H8 definitively and accept H14 as a dataset-supported association: KEAP1 loss is associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency. I will not infer canonical NRF2 biology or causality from this; it is an association in this dataset and may reflect data structure, coding convention, or context-specific behavior.

The two large positive discoveries remain solid within this dataset. H7 accepts that SMARCA4 loss is associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency: R7 signed estimate +0.7840, 95% interval +0.7646 to +0.8034, cell counts 412/1588. This is far above the approximate SMARCA2 10% threshold of 0.042 and biologically coherent with SWI/SNF synthetic lethality. H9 accepts that MSI-high is associated with stronger WRN dependency: R9 signed estimate +0.7899, interval +0.7604 to +0.8193, cell counts 130/1870. This also far exceeds the approximate WRN 10% threshold of 0.030. I keep both investigations active as main effects are accepted but should be checked for confounding by co-alterations and library/batch context.

The remaining driver/pathway tests are mostly unresolved. KRAS mutation versus KRAS dependency remains directionally supportive but imprecise, with interval crossing zero. EGFR amplification versus EGFR dependency is borderline and may become clearer in adenocarcinoma. ERBB2 amplification is near null but not tightly bounded. TP53 loss versus weaker MDM2 dependency remains small and imprecise. The Avana-library POLR2A benchmark shows no large scaling artifact but is unresolved. The rejected or not-supported hypotheses include stronger STAT3 dependency with KRAS mutation, stronger BRAF dependency with BRAF V600E in KRAS wildtype, and stronger DHX9 or RPL11 dependency with MYC amplification.

Next, I propose interaction and context refinements: whether the SMARCA4-SMARCA2 effect is modified by ARID1A co-loss, whether the reversed KEAP1-NFE2L2 association is modified by STK11 loss, and whether KRAS/EGFR direct dependencies become more interpretable within adenocarcinoma. These will be analyzed alongside registered refinements such as ARID1A loss versus SMARCA2, SMARCA4 effect within ARID1A-intact cells, Avana-only SMARCA4 effect, BRCA2 loss versus WRN, MSI-high excluding BRCA2 loss, MYC amplification versus TMED10, and TP53 loss versus USP7.

I register a second exploration batch aimed at three purposes: robustness of the accepted large associations, specificity and context dependence of borderline driver effects, and extension into untested dependency outcomes. Direction remains tied to the claim: for direction=-1, a positive signed estimate means the exposure is associated with a more negative dependency score, i.e. stronger dependency; for direction=+1, a positive signed estimate means a less negative score, i.e. weaker dependency. I will compare effect sizes to approximate 10% relative benchmarks derived from the population mean magnitude: about 0.042 for SMARCA2, 0.030 for WRN, 0.024-0.026 for most RTK/transcription/translation dependencies, and about 0.009 for NFE2L2/USP7.

First, accepted effects H7 and H9 should be stress-tested against technical structure. A batch-restricted test of SMARCA4 loss on SMARCA2 checks whether the enormous synthetic-lethal association is an artifact of one screening batch, while an Avana-restricted test of MSI-high on WRN checks whether the MSI-WRN association persists in the dominant library. These are not new biological hypotheses; they are falsification checks. If either association loses its magnitude or sign only within a major technical cell, I will downgrade its biological interpretation.

Second, I refine the SWI/SNF and RTK signals. ARID1A loss tested within SMARCA4-intact cells helps distinguish whether SMARCA2 dependency is a general SWI/SNF-loss effect or is especially tied to SMARCA4 loss. For RTK biology, ERBB2 and EGFR amplification effects are tested in KRAS wildtype contexts because KRAS-mutant signaling can bypass upstream receptor dependency and may mask RTK-specific effects. These should be interpreted as dataset-specific context refinements, not general oncogene-addiction claims.

Third, KRAS mutation effects are examined within STK11 wildtype and as a TP53 co-mutation interaction because co-alteration state can modify MAPK-pathway dependency. The KRAS main effect is borderline; these context tests may reveal whether the lack of a clinically large effect is dilution by heterogeneous co-mutation states. However, if intervals remain wide or effects remain small, I will not accept the main KRAS-dependency claim.

Fourth, I add two untested outcomes with plausible hypotheses. RIT1 is tested under the idea that KRAS-mutant cells may be less dependent on RIT1 because downstream RAS/MAPK signaling is already activated; this uses direction=+1, so a positive signed estimate supports weaker RIT1 dependency in KRAS mutants. KIF18A is tested with TP53 loss because p53-loss tumors may have increased chromosomal instability or mitotic stress and could be more dependent on a mitotic kinesin; this uses direction=-1 for stronger dependency. These are exploratory associations only.

Finally, I add a Ky-library POLR2A benchmark to complement the Avana benchmark. Library scaling can affect interpretation of accepted dependency scores, especially when library indicators are correlated with cell counts. If Ky-library POLR2A shows no large artifact, that strengthens confidence in using accepted associations; if it does, accepted claims should be rechecked by library. All claims remain dataset-specific associations until supported by validation or replication.

I request twelve discovery analyses focused on three priorities: (1) stress-test and localize the accepted large synthetic-lethal associations, (2) resolve whether borderline direct-driver effects become clearer in biologically motivated contexts, and (3) open two untested outcomes with plausible p53/RAS connections. For SMARCA2, H13 tests the direct ARID1A-loss association, H15 tests the SMARCA4-loss association within ARID1A-intact cells, and H25 tests SMARCA4-loss robustness within batch_a. These together distinguish whether SMARCA2 dependency is a general SWI/SNF-loss effect, whether it persists without ARID1A co-loss, and whether it is not confined to one screening batch. For WRN, H26 tests MSI-high dependency within the Avana library, H18 tests MSI-high after excluding BRCA2 loss to check whether the accepted MSI effect is confounded by repair-defining co-alterations, and H17 tests BRCA2 loss directly to see whether WRN dependency is also associated with another DNA-repair context. For RTK drivers, H24 tests EGFR amplification in adenocarcinoma, H28 tests EGFR amplification in KRAS wildtype, and H27 tests ERBB2 amplification in KRAS wildtype. These are context refinements where upstream RTK dependency may be less diluted by downstream RAS activation or subtype effects. Finally, H20 tests TP53 loss against USP7 dependency, a plausible p53-regulatory relationship and a bridge to the unresolved TP53-MDM2 signal; H32 tests KRAS mutation against RIT1 dependency, an untested outcome that may reflect alternative RAS-family signaling; and H33 tests TP53 loss against KIF18A dependency, a new mitotic-stress hypothesis. I defer the interaction tests H21 and H22, KRAS co-mutation interactions H29/H30, MYC-TMED10, and Ky-library POLR2A for later because this batch first tests direct specificity, major technical robustness, and high-information untested outcomes. All requested estimates are signed to the registered hypothesis direction and will be judged against approximate 10% relative benchmarks and uncertainty rather than causal interpretation.

I assessed all twelve newly delivered discovery results using the registered direction: for direction=-1 claims, a positive signed estimate means stronger dependency, while for direction=+1 claims, a positive signed estimate means weaker dependency. Because the task defines clinical significance as a relative difference of at least 10%, I used population outcome magnitudes as approximate absolute thresholds: SMARCA2 about 0.042, WRN about 0.030, USP7 about 0.009, and most other outcome scores about 0.024-0.026.

The new context and robustness results strengthen the two accepted large synthetic-lethal signals. H15 tests SMARCA4 loss within ARID1A-intact cells and gives a very large positive signed estimate +0.7770, 95% CI +0.7558 to +0.7983, with adequate cell counts 336/1253. This is far above the SMARCA2 clinical scale and supports accepting the SMARCA4-specific SMARCA2 association beyond general SWI/SNF co-loss. H25 tests SMARCA4 loss within batch_a: +0.7470, CI +0.7090 to +0.7850, n=113/406. This is smaller than the full-population effect but still enormous and precisely bounded above threshold, reducing concern that the main H7 effect is a single-batch artifact. Similarly, H26 tests MSI-high within the dominant Avana library: +0.7945, CI +0.7640 to +0.8250, n=120/1645. H18 tests MSI-high excluding BRCA2 loss: +0.7944, CI +0.7636 to +0.8252, n=121/1749. These support accepting H26 and H18 as active dataset-specific robustness/context refinements of H9. H17, direct BRCA2 loss versus WRN, is near null: signed -0.00008, CI -0.0449 to +0.0448. Its upper bound still crosses the WRN 10% scale, so I keep it unresolved rather than reject, but it currently does not support a clinically meaningful BRCA2-specific WRN effect.

H13 tests direct ARID1A loss versus SMARCA2 dependency: signed -0.0168, CI -0.0566 to +0.0229. The signed estimate is opposite the hypothesized stronger dependency, and the upper bound is well below the approximate 0.042 SMARCA2 threshold. Thus I reject the registered ARID1A->SMARCA2 stronger-dependency direction as unsupported in the overall dataset. This does not rule out a smaller or context-specific effect, but it is not a clinically meaningful discovery. H15 is more supportive because it isolates SMARCA4 loss among ARID1A-intact samples, and the remaining registered H31 can test ARID1A loss within SMARCA4-intact samples for specificity.

RTK context refinements do not yet become decisive. H24 adenocarcinoma EGFR amplification gives signed +0.0198, CI -0.0098 to +0.0494. It is directionally supportive but imprecise and zero is not excluded. H28 KRAS-wildtype EGFR amplification gives +0.0162, CI -0.0135 to +0.0459. These remain unresolved active; the intervals include clinically meaningful positive effects but do not exclude null or below-threshold effects. H27 KRAS-wildtype ERBB2 amplification gives signed -0.0093, CI -0.0424 to +0.0237. The interval does not support a clinically meaningful positive stronger-dependency effect, and the upper bound is below the approximate ERBB2 threshold, so I reject and close H27 in KRAS-wildtype. I do not interpret this as evidence that ERBB2 amplification is irrelevant generally; it is a negative result for this dataset-specific comparison.

The strongest new finding is H20: TP53 loss versus USP7 dependency, registered as weaker USP7 dependency with direction=+1. R23 gives signed +0.8019, CI +0.7823 to +0.8216, n=406/1594. Because USP7 has a small population mean magnitude around -0.093, the 10% threshold is only about 0.009. This effect is enormous and precisely bounded above that threshold. I accept H20 as a dataset association and request independent validation because it is new, biologically surprising, and large enough that validation can either strengthen it or reveal a coding/data-structure artifact. This is not yet a causal claim.

H32 KRAS mutation versus RIT1 dependency is small: signed +0.00365, CI -0.0147 to +0.0219. The upper bound is below the approximate RIT1 10% threshold, so I reject the proposed weaker-RIT1-dependency direction and close it. H33 TP53 loss versus stronger KIF18A dependency is directionally positive: signed +0.0208, CI +0.0012 to +0.0403. The point estimate is below the approximate KIF18A threshold of 0.0256, but the interval includes clinically meaningful positive values and narrowly excludes zero. I keep H33 unresolved active rather than accept; it is a possible p53/mitotic-stress association but not yet clinically meaningful beyond uncertainty.

For validation, I choose H20 rather than H15/H25/H26/H18 because the accepted synthetic-lethal effects already have multiple supporting robustness results, while H20 is a new large USP7 effect with only one discovery estimate. Independent validation of H20 is the most valuable use of the one voluntary validation request.

The new validation resolves the newly discovered USP7 association. H20 was registered with direction=+1, so a positive signed estimate means that TP53-loss samples have higher dependency_USP7 scores, i.e. weaker USP7 dependency because more negative scores indicate stronger dependency. Discovery R23 was signed +0.8019, 95% CI +0.7823 to +0.8216, n=406 versus 1594. The independent validation R26 is signed +0.8041, independent interval +0.7748 to +0.8334, n=389 versus 1611. Because the population mean magnitude of dependency_USP7 is only about 0.093, a 10% relative benchmark corresponds roughly to 0.009. The discovery and validation estimates are enormous relative to that scale and are concordant in sign, magnitude, and clinical relevance. I therefore accept H20 as a robust dataset-specific association: TP53 loss is associated with weaker USP7 dependency in this supplied dataset. I keep the investigation active while the already registered library, batch, and co-mutation context tests are evaluated, because a very large unexpected association still deserves context interrogation before broader interpretation. This is an association within the supplied dataset, not a causal claim, a claim of oncogenic mechanism, or a generalizable population finding.

The supported findings now separate into two accepted synthetic-lethal-like signals, one validated reversed KEAP1/NFE2L2 signal, and one newly validated TP53/USP7 signal. H7 accepts SMARCA4 loss as associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency: R7 signed +0.7840, CI +0.7646 to +0.8034, far above the approximate SMARCA2 10% benchmark of 0.042. The robustness results H15 and H25 strengthen this: within ARID1A-intact samples the signed estimate is +0.7770, CI +0.7558 to +0.7983; within batch_a it is +0.7470, CI +0.7090 to +0.7850. These support a dataset association that is not solely explained by ARID1A co-loss or by one screening batch. H9 accepts MSI-high as associated with stronger WRN dependency: R9 signed +0.7899, CI +0.7604 to +0.8193, far above the approximate WRN benchmark of 0.030. H26 and H18 add technical and confounding robustness: within the Avana library the signed estimate is +0.7945, CI +0.7640 to +0.8250, and after excluding BRCA2 loss it is +0.7944, CI +0.7636 to +0.8252. H14 accepts KEAP1 loss as associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, with discovery and independent validation both large and precisely signed. H20 now adds TP53 loss as associated with weaker USP7 dependency, with both discovery and independent validation showing similarly very large precise effects.

The negative findings remain important. H2 rejects KRAS mutation-associated stronger STAT3 dependency; R2 upper bound is well below the approximate STAT3 clinical benchmark. H5 rejects BRAF V600E-associated stronger BRAF dependency among KRAS-wildtype samples; R5 upper bound is below the approximate BRAF benchmark. H8 originally hypothesized that KEAP1 loss increases NFE2L2 dependency, but both discovery and validation reject that registered direction. H10 and H11 reject MYC amplification-associated stronger DHX9 or RPL11 dependency. H13 rejects ARID1A loss-associated stronger SMARCA2 dependency overall, because the upper confidence limit is below the approximate SMARCA2 benchmark; this negative finding does not exclude smaller or interaction-dependent ARID1A effects. H27 rejects ERBB2 amplification-associated stronger ERBB2 dependency in KRAS-wildtype samples for this dataset-specific comparison. H32 rejects KRAS mutation-associated weaker RIT1 dependency. These are conclusions about the tested comparisons in the supplied dataset, not definitive exclusions of all biological relevance in all contexts.

Several questions remain unresolved. H1 KRAS mutation versus stronger KRAS dependency is directionally supportive but imprecise and crosses zero. H3 EGFR amplification versus stronger EGFR dependency is borderline, with the lower confidence limit almost touching zero. H24 adenocarcinoma EGFR amplification and H28 KRAS-wildtype EGFR amplification are directionally supportive but not decisive. H33 TP53 loss versus stronger KIF18A dependency narrowly excludes zero but its point estimate is below the approximate KIF18A clinical benchmark, so it remains unresolved. Other deferred or unresolved effects include overall ERBB2 amplification, TP53 loss versus weaker MDM2 dependency, Avana-library POLR2A benchmark, and BRCA2 loss versus stronger WRN dependency. These are not accepted because their intervals include trivial effects, below-threshold effects, or both.

The most informative next analyses are context and technical-structure checks for the accepted effects, followed by focused driver refinements. For the new H20 association, the registered Avana-only and batch_a tests, the new non-Avana and batch_b tests, and KRAS-wildtype context tests will show whether the TP53-USP7 signal survives technical strata and co-mutation context. For SMARCA2, non-Avana and batch_b tests, together with registered H16, H31, and H21, will clarify whether the SMARCA4-SMARCA2 association is a broad library-robust association and whether ARID1A co-loss modifies it. For WRN, batch_b and additional batch tests will assess whether the MSI-WRN association is robust across screening batches. For driver biology, new EGFR and ERBB2 tests restricted to adenocarcinoma KRAS-wildtype samples may sharpen upstream receptor-dependency signals, and a KRAS test excluding BRAF V600E may reduce confounding by alternative RAS pathway activation. If these follow-ups preserve sign and magnitude, the accepted dataset associations can be treated as internally robust. If they materially shrink or reverse in a context, I will downgrade them to context-dependent or technically driven associations and avoid mechanistic interpretation.

I register a targeted exploration batch with three aims. First, I test whether the currently accepted large dataset associations are stable across the dominant CRISPR library. Library structure can shift CRISPR dependency scores and create artificial context dependence. For SMARCA4 loss on SMARCA2, KEAP1 loss on NFE2L2, and TP53 loss on USP7, I add Avana-versus-non-Avana interaction tests. These interactions ask whether the magnitude of the association itself changes by library, not merely whether the association remains present in one stratum. For direction=-1 claims, a positive signed interaction means the association is more negative-raw, i.e. stronger-dependency-aligned, in the Avana subgroup relative to the complement. For direction=+1 claims, a positive signed interaction means the association is higher-raw, i.e. weaker-dependency-aligned, in the Avana subgroup relative to the complement. I expect little modification if these effects are robust, but a large interaction would force a more context-dependent or technical interpretation.

Second, I test co-mutation independence for the accepted effects. TP53 loss, KEAP1 loss, SMARCA4 loss, and MSI-high may co-occur or share broader aneuploidy/defect states, so an apparent association with one dependency could be partly carried by another alteration. I register SMARCA4-loss effects in TP53 wildtype cells, TP53-loss USP7 effects in SMARCA4 wildtype cells, MSI-high WRN effects in TP53 wildtype cells, and KEAP1-loss NFE2L2 effects in TP53 wildtype cells. These are refinements of accepted claims. The expected directions follow the accepted dataset associations: stronger SMARCA2 dependency and WRN dependency, and weaker NFE2L2 and USP7 dependency. If an effect persists with similar magnitude, it becomes more internally specific; if it collapses in the wildtype context, I will downgrade the broader interpretation.

Third, I open new scientifically plausible predictor-outcome links. MYC amplification tested within TP53 wildtype cells targets the MYC-p53-MDM2 axis: MYC-driven p53 pathway activation could make cells more dependent on MDM2, so a more negative dependency_MDM2 score would support that hypothesis. EGFR amplification tested against TMED10 probes whether RTK-amplified cells are more dependent on secretory/Golgi trafficking machinery for signaling and growth. PIK3CA mutation tested against EGFR dependency in KRAS-wildtype adenocarcinoma probes downstream PI3K bypass: if PIK3CA mutation reduces receptor-level dependency, a higher, less negative EGFR dependency score would support weaker EGFR dependency. I also add a Humagne-library POLR2A benchmark to complement the Avana and Ky library checks, because POLR2A dependency could be distorted by library-specific normalization or screen artifacts.

Finally, I include research_marker_d_positive against SMARCA2 dependency as a negative-control specificity test. This marker is stated to have no assigned gene, pathway, or clinical role, so a large clinically meaningful association would suggest that unmodeled dataset structure could inflate apparent biology in this supplied dataset. A near-null or below-threshold result would modestly increase confidence that the accepted associations are not generic latent-marker artifacts. This control is not proposed as a biological claim.

These proposals remain dataset-specific association hypotheses. I will judge results against approximate 10% relative outcome scales, roughly 0.042 for SMARCA2, 0.030 for WRN, 0.009 for NFE2L2/USP7, and about 0.024-0.028 for most other outcomes, while considering uncertainty and context.

I select twelve analyses prioritized to stress-test the currently accepted large dataset associations and to provide a control for possible latent data structure. The accepted effects for SMARCA4 loss on SMARCA2, TP53 loss on USP7, and KEAP1 loss on NFE2L2 are so large that they must be interrogated for technical and co-mutation dependence before broader interpretation. I request direct non-Avana estimates for these three associations (H38, H41, H46) to determine whether the effects persist in the minority library stratum. I also request Avana-versus-non-Avana interaction tests (H48, H49, H50) to ask whether the association magnitude itself differs by library, rather than only whether it remains present. For direction=-1 claims, positive signed effects mean stronger-dependency-aligned differences; for direction=+1 claims, positive signed effects mean weaker-dependency-aligned differences. A large positive interaction for the direction=+1 USP7 and NFE2L2 claims would mean the weaker-dependency association is stronger in Avana than in non-Avana.

Next, I test co-mutation independence for the accepted effects. H52 tests SMARCA4-loss SMARCA2 association within TP53 wildtype cells; H53 tests MSI-high WRN association within TP53 wildtype cells; H54 tests KEAP1-loss NFE2L2 association within TP53 wildtype cells; and H51 tests TP53-loss USP7 association within SMARCA4 wildtype cells. These refinements ask whether each accepted association survives when a major co-altered pathway is held at wildtype or wildtype-like state. If the associations persist with similarly large effect sizes, they become more internally specific rather than mere markers of broad defect or co-alteration. If they collapse, I will downgrade them to context-dependent dataset associations.

I include H59 as a null-control/specificity check. Research marker D has no assigned gene, pathway, or clinical role; if it shows a very large clinically meaningful association with SMARCA2 dependency, this would indicate that unmodeled dataset structure may be generating large apparent effects and would require greater caution before interpreting the accepted associations biologically. If it is near null or below the approximate SMARCA2 10% scale of 0.042, that modestly increases confidence that the accepted associations are not generic latent-marker artifacts.

Finally, I include one new mechanistically motivated predictor-outcome test: H55 tests MYC amplification against stronger MDM2 dependency within TP53 wildtype cells. This addresses the known MYC-p53-MDM2 axis and may explain why the overall TP53-loss association with weaker MDM2 dependency was small and imprecise. In direction=-1 form, a positive signed estimate supports stronger MDM2 dependency in MYC-amplified, TP53 wildtype cells. I defer EGFR/TMED10, PIK3CA/EGFR context tests, and additional batch or library technical benchmarks for the next analysis round because the highest priority now is determining whether the current accepted large associations are robust across library structure, co-mutation context, and null-control background.

I assessed all newly delivered discovery results against the registered directions and the approximate 10% relative clinical scale. I used absolute outcome-magnitude benchmarks: SMARCA2 about 0.042, WRN about 0.030, USP7/NFE2L2 about 0.009, MDM2 about 0.027, and most other outcomes roughly 0.024-0.026. For direction=-1 outcomes, positive signed estimates mean stronger dependency; for direction=+1 outcomes, positive signed estimates mean weaker dependency.

The non-Avana library stress tests strengthen, rather than weaken, the accepted large dataset associations. H38 tests SMARCA4 loss versus SMARCA2 dependency within non-Avana screens. R27 is signed +0.8009, CI +0.7485 to +0.8534, n=61 versus 174. Although the exposed cell is small, the effect is enormous and precisely bounded above the SMARCA2 threshold. I accept H38 as a dataset-specific context association and keep it active because batch_b and broader technical context remain relevant. H41 tests TP53 loss versus USP7 dependency in non-Avana screens. R28 is signed +0.7674, CI +0.7031 to +0.8318, n=43 versus 192. This is far above the USP7 threshold of about 0.009 and supports the previously validated weaker-USP7-dependency association in the minority library stratum. I accept H41 as active. H46 tests KEAP1 loss versus NFE2L2 dependency in non-Avana screens. R29 is signed +0.7939, CI +0.7457 to +0.8422, n=40 versus 195, again far above the NFE2L2 threshold and supporting the reversed, validated direction of H14. I accept H46 as active. I do not interpret these as proving library-independent biology; rather, they reduce concern that the large effects are artifacts confined to the dominant Avana library.

The Avana-versus-non-Avana interaction tests are less decisive. H48 is a direction=-1 interaction for SMARCA4 loss on SMARCA2: positive signed interaction would mean the stronger-dependency association is more negative-raw in Avana relative to non-Avana. R30 is signed -0.0198, CI -0.0762 to +0.0365. The accepted context tests for the four large signals are robust, internally replicated, and partially directly validated already; additional validation would be redundant. Overall, the defensible conclusion is that the supplied dataset provides highly robust associations for SMARCA4 loss with stronger SMARCA2 dependency, MSI-high with stronger WRN dependency, KEAP1 loss with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, and TP53 loss with weaker USP7 dependency across high-Cas9 and adenocarcinoma strata, while the NF1-loss bypass hypothesis remains a promising unresolved dataset-specific signal and PTEN-loss weaker EGFR dependency is rejected in KRAS-wildtype adenocarcinoma.

The current supported scientific findings in this supplied lung-cell-line dataset are concentrated in four very large dependency associations. First, SMARCA4 loss is associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency. The overall comparison is accepted at +0.7840, and the exact ARID1A-intact context is now independently validated through H15/R15/R39. This gives a highly stable supplied-dataset signal, although it does not establish synthetic lethality causality or clinical applicability. Second, MSI-high is associated with stronger WRN dependency. The overall comparison is accepted at +0.7899, and the signal is large in Avana, BRCA2-intact, TP53-intact, KEAP1-intact, STK11-intact, high-Cas9, and adenocarcinoma contexts. Third, KEAP1 loss is associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, opposite the originally registered direction. H20 is accepted and independently validated through R26, and the effect remains very large in non-Avana, SMARCA4-intact, KEAP1-intact, high-Cas9, and adenocarcinoma contexts. The exact overall TP53-loss versus USP7-dependency question is now direct-validated; broader context tests remain descriptive and not necessary for establishing the main association. Across all four headline signals, the interpretation should be association within this supplied dataset, not causal inference and not external generalizability.

The dataset also provides informative negative or rejected findings for several canonical or constructed predictors. Unresolved uncertainty remains mainly in the driver, bypass, and technical-context programs. The overall KRAS-mutation effect on KRAS dependency is directionally consistent with stronger dependency but imprecise and below robust acceptance: +0.0137, interval -0.0038 to +0.0312. The most informative next analyses are mechanistic refinements rather than additional validation of the already accepted large signals. Secondary priority should be completing the already registered driver and context grid for unresolved canonical predictors, especially EGFR amplification in adenocarcinoma KRAS-wildtype cells, ERBB2 amplification in KRAS-wildtype contexts, KRAS-mutation effects stratified by subtype, BRAF background, STK11 status, and TP53 interaction, and PIK3CA/PTEN/ERBB2 bypass hypotheses. The accepted-signal context grid should be treated as descriptive completeness work: pending library, batch, subtype, and interaction tests may refine interpretation but are not necessary for the main conclusions. I would reserve validation budget for a new driver or specificity effect that is both precise and clinically meaningful, rather than for repeated validation of SMARCA4/SMARCA2, MSI/WRN, KEAP1/NFE2L2, or TP53/USP7.

Overall, the defensible report at this point is that the supplied dataset strongly and internally replicably associates four measured predictors with clinically large CRISPR dependency differences: SMARCA4 loss with stronger SMARCA2 dependency, MSI-high with stronger WRN dependency, KEAP1 loss with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, and TP53 loss with weaker USP7 dependency. The original KEAP1-loss stronger-NFE2L2 hypothesis is rejected, and several canonical driver and RTK bypass hypotheses remain negative, imprecise, or unresolved. No result should be stated as causal, clinically actionable, or generalizable beyond this dataset without external replication and experimental validation.

No assessments are due. For accepted headline signals, I registered missing genomic-context completeness tests: SMARCA4 loss among KRAS-mutant lines, MSI-high among KRAS-mutant lines, KEAP1 loss among TP53-loss lines, and TP53 loss among KEAP1-loss lines. No validation budget is requested at this stage. The priority is to determine whether PTEN-loss EGFR specificity tests remain clinically meaningful and pathway-specific, and whether new predictor discoveries are robust, before spending independent validation on a new signal.

This failure downgrades the PTEN-loss EGFR-dependency program. The PTEN specificity controls also remain informative for interpretation but not decisive. The overall dataset-specific scientific picture now separates into robust accepted associations, robust negative or validation-failed signals, and unresolved borderline signals. Accepted supplied-dataset associations remain dominated by very large effects: SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, including validated ARID1A-wildtype and many context refinements; MSI-high is associated with much stronger WRN dependency; KEAP1 loss is associated with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, with the original stronger-NFE2L2 direction rejected; and TP53 loss is associated with much weaker USP7 dependency, validated independently. These associations are not causal or generalizable claims; they are dataset-specific patterns.

Negative or validation-failed signals now include H95, where NF1-loss associated weaker KRAS dependency in KRAS/BRAF-wildtype cells failed independent validation, leading to rejection and downgrading of the NF1 bypass program; H10, where MYC amplification associated stronger DHX9 dependency failed independent validation; H105, PTEN-loss associated stronger EGFR dependency in high-Cas9 KRAS-wildtype adenocarcinoma; H109, PTEN-loss associated weaker KRAS dependency; H122 and H123, which reject broad POLR2A shifts for SMARCA4 loss and KEAP1 loss and therefore support some outcome specificity of those large signals; and other exact context rejections such as ERBB2 amplification in the KRAS-wildtype adenocarcinoma high-Cas9 context H102.

Unresolved uncertainty remains around several smaller signals. EGFR amplification-associated stronger EGFR dependency in H3, H24, and H28 is near threshold in some contexts but not supported with acceptable uncertainty. KRAS mutation-associated stronger KRAS dependency remains weakly imprecise. KIF18A TP53-loss signals H33, H115, and H116 are borderline or near null, so the KIF18A program is not established. POLR2A TP53-loss H124 remains unresolved because its interval includes clinically meaningful values, motivating the new high-Cas9 POLR2A specificity test. The accepted-signal robustness proposals for high-Cas9 adenocarcinoma are next useful analyses to test whether the large accepted associations persist simultaneously in the most favorable subtype and screening-quality context, while existing untested context-completeness claims H117-H121, STAT3 SMAD4 H125, PTEN KRAS-mutant specificity H111, and marker controls H78/H79 remain useful for negative-control and boundary testing. Overall, the most scientifically meaningful supported findings are still the four large dependency-specific associations; the new PTEN EGFR validation does not add a new supported finding and redirects effort toward coherence and specificity rather than further PTEN pursuit.

No validation is requested in this exploration stage because no new discovery result yet exceeds clinical-scale support with acceptable uncertainty; analysis should first determine whether these new context and specificity tests produce any candidate signal worth validation.

No assessments are due. The four accepted dataset-specific dependency programs remain internally validated: SMARCA4 loss associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency, MSI-high associated with stronger WRN dependency, KEAP1 loss associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, and TP53 loss associated with weaker USP7 dependency. These remain associations in the supplied dataset, not causal or externally generalizable claims. Signed convention remains: for direction -1, a positive returned estimate means the exposed group has a stronger, more negative dependency score; for direction +1, a positive returned estimate means the exposed group has a weaker, less negative dependency score. Approximate 10-percent clinical scales remain about 0.042 for SMARCA2, 0.030 for WRN, 0.009 for NFE2L2, 0.009 for USP7, and 0.025 to 0.026 for KIF18A, POLR2A, and RPL11. The first two proposals are focused boundary tests. KIF18A TP53-loss dependency in high-Cas9 Avana adenocarcinoma screens refines the near-threshold KIF18A signal: a robust positive signed effect above about 0.025 would support TP53 loss associated with stronger KIF18A dependency in a high-quality adenocarcinoma context, while an interval crossing zero or remaining near threshold would keep this claim unresolved. SMARCA4-loss SMARCA2 dependency under low Cas9 activity tests whether the very large SMARCA2 program persists when screening quality is lower; persistence would reduce concern that it is restricted to high-Cas9 contexts, while attenuation would identify technical context dependence. The next four proposals are pre-specified phenotype-state interaction tests within high-quality Avana contexts. SMARCA2 is tested in high versus low EMT state, WRN in high versus low EMT state, NFE2L2 in high versus low hypoxia state, and USP7 in high versus low stemness state. The main hypotheses are that EMT-high state strengthens the SMARCA4-loss SMARCA2 effect, hypoxia-high state amplifies KEAP1-loss weaker NFE2L2 dependency, and stemness-high state amplifies TP53-loss weaker USP7 dependency; WRN is registered with uncertain state modification because the MSI-high effect could be either chromatin-remodeling-specific or broadly proliferation-associated. A positive signed interaction in the accepted program direction means the effect is larger in the high-state subgroup than in its complement; a near-null interaction favors context stability. The remaining six proposals are cross-predictor and broad-essentiality specificity controls in high-Cas9 Avana screens. KEAP1 loss versus USP7 and TP53 loss versus NFE2L2 test whether the accepted oxidative-stress and p53-associated effects cross into the other stress dependency program. SMARCA4 loss versus WRN and MSI-high versus SMARCA2 test whether the large SMARCA2 and WRN programs spill over to non-matched outcomes. TP53 loss versus RPL11 and SMARCA4 loss versus POLR2A test whether accepted predictors also shift broadly essential transcription or ribosomal dependency programs. Clinically large non-matched or essentiality effects would weaken narrow interpretation of the accepted programs; near-null or below-threshold intervals would support outcome specificity, although wide intervals should remain unresolved rather than be accepted as definitive specificity proof. No validation is requested during exploration; validation should be considered at appraisal only if a new focused follow-up is robust and clinically sized.

No assessments are due. I requested twelve untested existing claims to concentrate on high-quality screening contexts, unresolved near-threshold signals, and specificity controls. Signed convention: for direction -1, a positive signed estimate means the exposed group has a stronger, more negative dependency score; for direction +1, a positive signed estimate means the exposed group has a weaker, less negative dependency score. Approximate 10-percent clinical scales are about 0.0415 for SMARCA2, 0.030 for WRN, 0.009 for NFE2L2, 0.009 for USP7, 0.025-0.027 for POLR2A/RPL11/MAM2-like moderate outcomes, and about 0.025 for KIF18A, EGFR, and KRAS. H158 and H165 test the near-threshold KIF18A TP53-loss association in Avana high-Cas9 screens overall and in adenocarcinoma, respectively: a clinically robust positive signed estimate with lower bound above threshold would support a TP53-loss KIF18A association, while crossing null or remaining near threshold keeps it unresolved. Persistence would reduce concern that these headline associations are Avana-library artifacts; attenuation would mark technical context dependence. I assessed the newly delivered discovery evidence under the existing signed convention: for direction -1, a positive estimate means the exposed group has stronger, more negative dependency; for direction +1, a positive estimate means the exposed group has weaker, less negative dependency. No new claim met the bar for acceptance. The most notable result is H165: TP53 loss was associated with stronger KIF18A dependency in high-Cas9 Avana adenocarcinoma screens, with signed estimate +0.0299, interval -0.00009 to +0.0599. The point estimate exceeds the approximate KIF18A clinical scale of about 0.025-0.026, but the interval includes zero by a negligible amount and the claim remains post hoc refinement of earlier near-threshold TP53-KIF18A signals. Because the subgroup/context selection could increase false-positive risk, I kept H165 unresolved and requested independent validation rather than accepting it. H158, the same predictor-outcome pair in the broader high-Cas9 Avana context, was weaker and non-significant: +0.0201, interval -0.0048 to +0.0449. Its point is below the clinical threshold and crosses null, so it remains unresolved but deferred; if H165 validation succeeds, H158 can be reassessed as a broader but less clean context. The other new positive near-null tests are not clinically compelling: H159 EGFR amplification in high-quality adenocarcinoma KRAS-wildtype Avana screens gave +0.0061 with interval -0.0370 to +0.0492; H160 KRAS mutation in high-quality adenocarcinoma Avana screens gave +0.0165 with interval -0.0103 to +0.0433; H164 TP53 loss on MDM2 in high-Cas9 Avana screens gave +0.0249 with interval -0.0069 to +0.0567. All cross null and/or have point estimates at or below the relevant 10-percent scale, so they remain unresolved and deferred. The specificity controls remain inconclusive rather than definitive. H173 SMARCA4 loss versus WRN gave a small negative point, -0.0037, interval -0.0425 to +0.0350, but the upper bound reaches clinically meaningful positive effects; H174 MSI-high versus SMARCA2 gave +0.0446, near threshold but interval -0.0407 to +0.1299, so it remains active only as an uncertainty because the point is near the SMARCA2 clinical scale though extremely imprecise. H175 TP53 loss versus RPL11 and H176 SMARCA4 loss versus POLR2A were near null but their upper bounds include or nearly include meaningful positive effects. These controls neither support cross-program effects nor establish strong specificity. The three non-Avana high-Cas9 boundary checks H161-H163 had insufficient cell counts in every cell, with cells 10/34, 7/37, and 10/34 respectively. These invalid results provide no evidence for or against library dependence, so I closed those exact boundary tests as data-limited rather than interpreting them as attenuation or persistence. Overall, the four large validated programs remain unchanged. The only promising new follow-up is H165, which warrants independent validation before any acceptance.

Signed convention remains unchanged: for direction -1, a positive returned estimate means the exposed group has stronger, more negative CRISPR dependency; for direction +1, a positive returned estimate means the exposed group has weaker, less negative dependency. The independent validation intervals use adjusted alpha around 0.003846 to account for multiple validations. Approximate 10-percent clinical scales are about 0.0415 for SMARCA2, 0.030 for WRN, 0.009 for NFE2L2, 0.009 for USP7, 0.027 for MDM2, and 0.0256 for KIF18A. H9: MSI-high versus non-MSI-high on WRN dependency is robustly confirmed by independent validation. Discovery R9 was +0.790 with lower bound +0.760; validation R103 is +0.822 with adjusted lower bound +0.768 and upper +0.875. This is far above the WRN clinical scale and in the anticipated stronger-dependency direction, so I accept and close the exact headline claim. H106: TP53 loss versus TP53-intact on MDM2 dependency in the selected adenocarcinoma KRAS-wild-type context remains unsupported. Discovery R75 was only +0.0069 with interval -0.0286 to +0.0424, below the MDM2 clinical scale and crossing null. Independent validation R104 is in the opposite direction, -0.0301, with adjusted interval -0.0808 to +0.0206. The validation upper bound for the anticipated positive/weaker-dependency direction is below the approximate clinical threshold, so a clinically meaningful TP53-loss weaker MDM2 dependency in that exact context is not supported. The opposite-direction point is interesting but its interval still includes null, so I do not create a new opposite claim from this alone; I reject and close the original H106 direction. H165: TP53 loss versus intact on KIF18A dependency in high-Cas9 Avana adenocarcinoma was a post hoc near-threshold discovery refinement. Discovery R119 was +0.0299, just above the KIF18A clinical scale, but the 95 percent interval was -0.00009 to +0.0599, meaning the null was not cleanly excluded. Independent validation R130 is much weaker: +0.0138 with adjusted interval -0.0327 to +0.0603. The validation point is below the clinical threshold, the interval crosses null, and the interval still permits a clinically meaningful positive effect, so this exact context cannot be accepted. Because this was a selected subgroup and the independent test failed to reproduce the near-threshold result, I keep the exact claim unresolved but close this selected context for further work. H14: the reversed KEAP1-loss NFE2L2 claim, TP53/KEAP1 oxidative-stress program aside, remains accepted as KEAP1 loss associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency. Discovery R8 and validation R13 are about +0.796 and +0.810 signed, far above the NFE2L2 clinical scale, so I close the exact headline claim as validated. Scientific synthesis: the four large dataset-specific dependency programs remain supported by independent validation where applicable: SMARCA4 loss associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency, MSI-high associated with much stronger WRN dependency, KEAP1 loss associated with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, and TP53 loss associated with much weaker USP7 dependency. These are associations in the supplied dataset and should not be interpreted as causal or externally generalizable claims. Negative or unsupported selected contexts include the high-quality adenocarcinoma KRAS-wild-type PTEN-loss EGFR context, NF1-loss KRAS selected context, MYC amplification effects on DHX9, MYC amplification effects on RPL11, broad POLR2A TP53-loss weaker control, PTEN-loss EGFR high-quality selected direction in H105, and TP53-loss MDM2 selected direction in H106. Constructed-marker null controls generally behaved as expected, but marker effects should not be given biological interpretation because the markers were constructed without assigned biological role. Unresolved uncertainty remains mainly around modest effects near clinical thresholds. Broad TP53 loss versus KIF18A is the most important unresolved KIF18A signal: H33 has point estimate +0.0208 with interval +0.0012 to +0.0403, so it excludes null but has a point estimate below the 10-percent scale and interval extending above threshold; H158 in high-Cas9 Avana contexts is also near threshold but crosses null. The selected adenocarcinoma refinement in H165 did not validate and should be deprioritized. Modest positive trends for KRAS mutation on KRAS dependency, EGFR amplification on EGFR dependency, ERBB2 amplification on ERBB2 dependency, and NF1 loss on KRAS dependency remain unresolved or rejected in selected contexts and should not be elevated without tighter estimates or independent confirmation. Specificity controls for the accepted programs remain imperfect: some controls are near null but have intervals that still allow clinically meaningful cross effects, so they support specificity only weakly. The most informative next analysis is to use any remaining validation capacity on the pre-specified broad TP53-loss KIF18A claim H33 rather than on the failed selected H165 context. Acceptance would require an independent interval excluding null and, ideally, a lower bound above the KIF18A clinical threshold; failure would close the broader KIF18A hypothesis as not clinically supported in this dataset. Secondary next analyses should focus on pre-registered specificity controls, library and Cas9 boundary tests that have adequate cell counts, and untested state-interaction tests only if they can be interpreted without post hoc subgroup selection.
